observed: The tracking tolerance sigma is derived under two different kernels in two places. One set of the project's working notes states it is the sigma in a GAUSSIAN exp(-|v-v_cmd|^2/sigma^2); research/scripts/measure_tracking_noise.py derives it under a CAUCHY Phi(u)=1/(1+u^2), and the 3x rule's 0.900 floor score is Cauchy-specific. research/CORE_PLAN.md:162 uses the Gaussian with sigma~0.25 m/s, flagged as a guess.
where: project working notes vs research/scripts/measure_tracking_noise.py:21-40 vs research/CORE_PLAN.md:162
why_it_matters: At the noise floor the two kernels agree to within 0.005 (Cauchy 0.900 vs Gaussian 0.895), so the disagreement is invisible exactly where anyone would check it. At 3 sigma they differ by three orders of magnitude (0.100 vs 1.2e-4) -- and the tail is where the whole 'does an uncontrolled machine farm the turning term?' question lives. A cycle could adopt the measured sigma under the wrong kernel and get a reward that pays 85% for no yaw control.
cheapest_next_step: state the kernel explicitly wherever sigma appears, and record the chosen one in the reward spec. The design cycle must pick one and say why; nothing in the repo currently records that a choice was ever made.
resolution: Closed 2026-07-27 by cycle 006's build, and noticed by cycle 007's recall rather than by anyone revisiting this row. The kernel is now stated in all three places the row asked for. (1) research/measurements/tracking_noise.json states it as its FIRST key: 'cauchy: Phi(u) = 1/(1+u^2)', beside floor_score_under_kernel 0.9 and the sigma = 3 * floor rule. (2) The reward spec records it: config.json reward_spec.terms[track_cmd].params carries kernel='cauchy' and frame='heading', and both are inside the reward hash e374eb2def4e6fc9, so a silent kernel swap changes the hash and reward-spec fails. (3) The tracking-frame guard asserts the kernel numerically -- Phi(1)=0.500000 against the Gaussian's 0.367879 -- so the two cannot be confused at the 3-sigma tail where they differ by three orders of magnitude. CORE_PLAN.md:162's Gaussian sigma~0.25 guess was superseded by sigma_v=0.15, sigma_w=0.1 under Cauchy.

what: track_eval's EVAL_GRID scores the policy on the command (-0.3, 0, 0), but the env's BACKWARD command floor is 0.40. It is not obviously a large error -- the module docstring already refuses to evaluate a policy trained with zero-filled command slots for exactly this reason, and this is a milder version of the same objection -- but it is the same class of mistake. It also biases in a KNOWN direction: -0.3 is the easiest backward command in the grid, and standing's creep is backward at -0.03553 m/s, so this is the cell where a do-nothing machine does relatively best. The options are (a) leave it and document that cell 3 is off-manifold, (b) add a parallel grid and report both, (c) move it to -0.4 and re-measure both zero-action baselines, accepting that older numbers become unquotable. Do not silently edit the constant.

what: Cycle 012 proposed that guard vacuity is a function of a guard's AGE. Measured across all 16 guards (record.guard_birth_audit), the proposal survives but the MECHANISM is wrong. Of the 11 testable guards, 5 were born vacuous and 6 born covering, and the split is not by age -- the whole suite spans 51 hours, so age barely varies. It splits by WHAT THE SET IS: all 6 born-covering guards quantify over a category that already existed (runs/, ledger rows, nulls rows); all 5 born-vacuous guards quantify over a FIELD THE GUARD ITSELF INVENTED (obs_spec, reward_spec, terrain_spec, best_eval_episodes, a measurement sha256). why_it_matters: It changes what the loop should DO about vacuity. Under the age model, waiting fixes it and nothing is owed. Under the field-invention model, a guard that demands a new field is vacuous until a PRODUCER is wired, which is a task with an owner, not weather -- and it predicts which guards will be born vacuous BEFORE they ship. It also weakens the reassurance cycle 012 took from `measurement-provenance` being merely young: at 1.7 h it sits below the whole observed band, so its 3 vacuous assertions are not yet evidence either way.
not_chased_because: the data cannot settle it and this cycle's experiment was the harvest. n=11, one repository, 51 hours of guard history, and 5 of the 5 supporting points are RECONSTRUCTED rather than observed -- `n` did not exist as a field until cycle 011, so no one ever saw checkpoint-width render VACUOUS. falsifier: The model dies if a guard stays vacuous while data of its declared type accumulates. Concretely: if >=3 new measurement JSONs naming checkpoints are written after 2026-07-28T06:25 and measurement-provenance is STILL vacuous, emptiness is design rather than shipping latency. what: WebFetch against a RAW arXiv PDF url returns undecodable binary, and the summarising model then CONFABULATES specific numeric values that contradict the same paper's own HTML rendering. Observed on arXiv 2310.12931v2, where a PDF fetch produced per-task figures disagreeing with the paper's HTML; caught only because the same numbers were pulled a second time from a different rendering and compared. The failure is silent: the answer comes back fluent, specific, and attached to a real URL.
why_it_matters: This is a mechanism for putting INVENTED numbers into an append-only record, which is precisely what the number rule exists to prevent. A confabulated figure arrives with a citation already attached, so it reads as fully sourced and will be quoted by later cycles that do not re-derive it. It is the literature-sweep analogue of anomalies 20/23/27: a number that looks provenanced and cannot be reproduced. Note the asymmetry -- a raw-PDF fetch that exceeds the content-length limit fails LOUDLY (observed the same day on arXiv 2109.11978, which returned a maxContentLength error), and that is the safe case. The dangerous case is the fetch that appears to succeed.
cheapest_next_step: Never cite a number taken from a raw PDF fetch. Use ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/<id> or arxiv.org/html/<id>v<n>, which return real text; where a figure is load-bearing, fetch it twice from different renderings and compare before it enters the record. Both reward tables in decisions/0004 that came from papers were pulled this way, and the Rudin table was fetched twice for that reason.

what: The '152x' figure in circulation for Newton / MuJoCo-Warp is measured against MJX, not against PhysX, and it is not the locomotion-training benchmark it is usually cited as. Primary source is a dated vendor engineering blog (2025-09-29): 'MuJoCo Warp, the main Newton solver, is up to 152x faster for locomotion...than MJX on GeForce RTX 4090'. The only PhysX comparison on that same page is 'up to 65% faster in-hand dexterous manipulation with MuJoCo Warp versus PhysX' -- manipulation, not locomotion. As of 2026-07-29 NO Newton-vs-PhysX locomotion benchmark exists publicly; the Isaac Lab benchmark harness for it is still open work. The blog's own quadruped example is ANYmal-D at 4096 envs on FLAT RIGID TERRAIN ONLY, with no throughput, VRAM or wall-clock reported.
why_it_matters: Any expectation of a large Newton speedup for rough-terrain locomotion rests on a number measured against a different baseline (MJX, not PhysX) on a different axis. Two further facts compound it. First, there is no final Isaac Lab v3.0.0: the newest release is v3.0.0-beta2.patch1 (2026-07-02), whose notes say the branch may still receive breaking changes before final -- the in-tree version string reads 3.0.0, which is why an installed environment reports it as released. Second, the height scanner on the Newton path is genuinely unresolved: the beta2 release notes claim ray-caster support while the Newton limitations page omits it. what: The alpha_w derivation conditioned its noise floor on the WRONG ARM: docs/theory/command-tracking-reward.md section 2 and the ALPHA_W_MIN window in src/bestiary/envs/hound_track_rel.py both feed the STANDING yaw noise floor (0.0182 rad/s, research/measurements/tracking_noise.json) into the noise side of the two-sided rule, but Phi_w is scored while DRIVING. Learning 012's own inversion of the best crash-free driving cell (Phi_w = 0.6052 at alpha=1.0, 0.30 m/s) implies a driving residual of 0.10*sqrt(1/0.6052-1) = 0.0808 rad/s, 4.4x the standing floor. Redone on the driving-conditioned arm, the window is: noise side alpha_w >= 3*0.0808 = 0.242; freeride side (unsteered 0.127 rad/s must score <= 0.45) alpha_w <= 0.127/sqrt(ln(1/0.45)) = 0.142. The window [0.242, 0.142] is EMPTY -- no alpha_w satisfies both bounds at measured residuals.
why_it_matters: A published derivation this project relies on -- the one that produced alpha_w = 0.10 -- was computed on the wrong conditional, and the defect explains a measured result without invoking undertraining: the noise-only ceiling E[exp(-w^2/alpha^2)] = 1/sqrt(1+2s^2/alpha^2) at s = 0.0808, alpha = 0.10 is 0.659, against learning 012's measured 0.6052 (gap = the bias component). The 'Phi_w ceiling' of 012 is the kernel's own noise ceiling, computed. The rate-domain yaw objective is infeasible unless a controller reaches a driving residual below 0.142/3 = 0.047 rad/s, which no measured policy approaches. The moving-phase SPEED noise floor has the same conditioning gap (command-tracking-reward.md section 7.4 flags it unmeasured) and should be presumed suspect until measured.
cheapest_next_step: No new run needed for the diagnosis -- the arithmetic above is closed. Two follow-ups: (1) integrate the yaw traces already in run logs to measure the wobble spectrum and whether 0.0808 is bias or noise (one script, no GPU); (2) the proposed structural repair -- close the loop through the command, production-style -- is derived in docs/theory/reward-composition.md section 5 and must ride its own arm under learnings/004.
found_by: the 2026-07-29 reward-mathematics deep review, re-deriving the two-sided window against learnings 011/012/015
refutation: WITHDRAWN -- 'infeasible as specified' is wrong. The 0.0808 rad/s driving residual was placed on the NOISE side of the two-sided rule. docs/theory/command-tracking-reward.md section 2 had already considered and explicitly rejected that substitution in writing: a driving residual is unremovable noise PLUS the error the policy exists to remove, so it belongs on the freeride side as a thing to EXCLUDE, never on the noise side as a thing to TOLERATE. It bounds the noise floor from ABOVE, not below, and it is one undertrained non-converged single-seed probe. Corrected window: [3n, 0.0905] where n is the driving-conditioned unremovable noise floor and has NEVER been measured -- UNPINNED, not empty. Two compounding defects: the 3x multiplier is this repo's own convention and the window is empty only if it exceeds 1.760; and the two sides were computed on different statistical arms (mean kernel vs point kernel on an rms), the exact error learnings/012 warns about. The 0.659 'confirming' ceiling also used a GAUSSIAN expectation against a Phi_w measured under the CAUCHY kernel -- the right kernel gives 0.7203, further from 0.6052, and is circular anyway. Measuring n is the whole question, and no committed artifact holds a raw yaw trace: track_eval.py:314 records achieved_vx only.

what: The SHIPPED alpha_w = 0.10 fails its own freeride cap when the cap is evaluated on the arm the reward actually pays. src/bestiary/envs/hound_track_rel.py:155 comments that the unsteered freerider 'scores that freeride at 0.20, comfortably tighter than the 0.45 cap' -- that is a POINT kernel applied to an rms yaw rate. what: The inherited Isaac locomotion command set asks a wheel-legged robot for a velocity it cannot produce. velocity_env_cfg.py:140-151 samples lin_vel_y from (-1.0, 1.0) m/s in the BODY frame, and track_lin_vel_xy_exp (isaaclab/envs/mdp/rewards.py:314-325) sums e_x^2 + e_y^2 inside one exponent with std^2 = 0.25. Hound's four wheels all spin about +Y (build.py, CARD.md:117), the tyre contact is condim=3 so sliding friction is isotropic at mu = 0.9, and the CARD itself says a wheel 'rolls fore-aft but GRIPS sideways'. Sustained body-frame lateral velocity is therefore unavailable except by lifting wheels and shuffling on abduction, nowhere near 1 m/s. Roughly 80% of the 2-D command square asks for motion the machine cannot make. Computed consequence (scratch script, NOT yet committed, so uncitable under the number rule): if v_y == 0 is the only achievable lateral behaviour, the best attainable value of track_lin_vel_xy_exp is E_c[exp(-(c_y/0.5)^2)] = 0.441, so 56% of the largest reward term's income is unattainable at any competence. The same 0.441 is what makes the 2-D best-command-blind figure 0.4409^2 = 0.194 look like a strong freeride fence: the fake and the honest tracker are crushed by the same impossible axis, and fake/achievable is 0.441, not 0.194.
where: src/bestiary/isaac/anymal_desert_env_cfg.py inherits AnymalCRoughEnvCfg's CommandsCfg unchanged; the reward term is IsaacLab's track_lin_vel_xy_exp. Found while refuting the Hound Isaac design pass, 2026-07-29.
why_it_matters: This is learnings/011's punished-for-unremovable-error shape one level up, sitting on the term the whole reward table is built around, and it silently inflates every freeride number computed against that command set -- including the figure offered as the ground for choosing additive over multiplicative composition (decisions/0005). It also means the command distribution, not the kernel, is where the design error lives, which is exactly the axis learnings/015 identified and the axis nobody re-checked when the platform changed from a legged reference robot (which can crab) to a wheel-legged one (which cannot).
cheapest_next_step: No GPU training. One rollout on the Isaac desert commanding pure lateral velocity (v_x = 0, v_y sweeping 0 -> 1 m/s, yaw 0) and reporting the largest sustained body-frame |v_y| the machine holds; a zero-command lateral-push rollout bounds it from the other side. Minutes. That number sets the command range, and the command range must be set BEFORE the reward table is fixed, because narrowing lin_vel_y to +-0.2 moves the 2-D freeride figure from 0.194 to 0.419 and changes the composition arithmetic again.

where: src/bestiary/terrain/isaac_hf.py:167-244 (ranking and difficulty indexing), src/bestiary/isaac/anymal_desert_env_cfg.py:70-97 (TILE_M 8.0, border_width 0.25), assets/terrain/desert_hfield.bin, against IsaacLab's terrain_levels_vel promote/demote at .../velocity/mdp/curriculums.py:42-54.

what: The four-quadrant torque-speed actuator model is dead code on the robot whose measurement anchors every Isaac number we have. DCMotor._clip_effort (isaaclab/actuators/actuator_pd.py:295-307) computes torque_speed_top = saturation_effort * (1 - joint_vel/velocity_limit) and the matching bottom envelope, so the curve is a line of slope -saturation_effort/velocity_limit flat-topped at +-effort_limit. But ANYmal-C uses ANYDRIVE_3_LSTM_ACTUATOR_CFG (isaaclab_assets/robots/anymal.py:122), and ActuatorNetLSTM.compute (isaaclab/actuators/actuator_net.py:77-98) OVERRIDES DCMotor.compute and never assigns self._joint_vel. DCMotor.compute does assign it (actuator_pd.py:286-289) and ActuatorNetMLP.compute does (actuator_net.py:157); the LSTM path does not. _joint_vel is allocated as zeros in DCMotor.__init__ (actuator_pd.py:272) and _clip_effort only ever writes a clipped version of itself back. So with joint_vel identically zero the envelope collapses to torque_speed_top = 120*(1-0) = 120 -> clip(max=80) = 80 and the bottom to -80: a flat, velocity-independent +-80 N.m. Read from source only; not executed at runtime.
where: installed Isaac Lab tree, VERSION 3.0.0 (release/3.0.0-beta2). Relevant to Bestiary because Bestiary-Desert-Coarse-Anymal-C-v0 is the only Isaac configuration this project has measured, and every throughput and VRAM figure in the record comes from it.
why_it_matters: The design pass named DCMotorCfg as the fix for maneuver realism -- 'the sim must model the tau-omega line or every maneuver result is fiction' -- while the baseline it inherited its numbers from silently has no tau-omega line at all. Three consequences. (1) Any maneuver conclusion drawn on ANYmal-C would be drawn under an ideal flat-torque actuator, the exact fiction the fix was meant to remove. (2) The planned A0 control arm cannot be a one-variable change: ANYmal-C's LSTM actuator net cannot port to Hound, so A0 changes the body AND the actuator model AND the reward body-name regexes. (3) A DCMotorCfg for Hound must be verified to actually bite -- writing the config is not evidence the curve is active, since here it is configured and inert.
cheapest_next_step: No GPU. When a Hound articulation cfg is written, assert the envelope empirically rather than trusting the config: step the articulation at several joint velocities under a saturating command and check that applied torque falls with speed. Two lines in an oracle. Separately, re-read this from an in-scope copy of the actuator source before it is cited in a learning, and check whether upstream has an issue open on the missing _joint_vel assignment.

what: The inherited domain-randomization table does not randomize friction. velocity_env_cfg.py:200-210 sets physics_material with static_friction_range = (0.8, 0.8), dynamic_friction_range = (0.6, 0.6), restitution_range = (0.0, 0.0) and num_buckets = 64. All three ranges are DEGENERATE: the event sets friction to a constant rather than sampling it, and num_buckets = 64 is therefore inert. Two adjacent terms in the same EventCfg are also weaker than they look: base_external_force_torque has force_range = (0.0, 0.0) and torque_range = (-0.0, 0.0), i.e. a no-op placeholder; and reset_robot_joints' position_range = (0.5, 1.5) is a MULTIPLICATIVE scale on the default joint position (isaaclab/envs/mdp/events.py:1924-1962), so any joint whose default is exactly 0 is unrandomized by construction.
where: installed Isaac Lab tree, inherited unchanged by src/bestiary/isaac/anymal_desert_env_cfg.py (which overrides only scene.terrain.terrain_generator).
why_it_matters: It changes the shape of the low-mu gap from 'the range is narrow' to 'there is no range', which makes the traction arm cheaper to justify and more urgent: at mu = 0.3 the per-wheel traction limit is mu*M*g*r/4 = 1.06 N.m against a 3.0 N.m gear, so wheelspin becomes reachable and slip becomes stochastic -- and nothing in the inherited table ever shows the policy a surface where that is true. It also means any sim-to-sim or sim-to-real robustness claim made from this config is a claim about one friction pair, not a range. The multiplicative joint reset is a second silent one: it reads as broad randomization and does nothing at all for zero-default joints, which for Hound would be abduction (stance_abduct = 0.0).
cheapest_next_step: No GPU. In the Hound env cfg, widen static_friction_range to about (0.2, 1.0) in the terrain and payload arms, and treat friction as a declared arm variable rather than an inherited default. Before adding any slip REWARD term, add the instrument: longitudinal slip s = v_axle - omega*r_w logged per wheel. Note envs/hound.py:576 already has the MuJoCo twin (rolling_fraction) and NO measured value of it appears anywhere in the record -- see the dead-instrumentation caveat there (hardcoded r = 0.085, gated to 0.0 below 0.2 m/s, x_velocity only).

what: The first Isaac Hound training run was NOT asymmetric actor-critic, although rsl_rl supports it and the literature this reward was inherited from uses it. Two independent reasons, both read from the installed Isaac Lab 3.0.0-beta2 tree (commit af1bab4dc173ba69b08fab779c14ead61d13fd33). (1) obs_groups is declared MISSING in the base config (isaaclab_rl/rsl_rl/rl_cfg.py:252) and AnymalCRoughPPORunnerCfg never sets it, while the sibling AnymalDRoughPPORunnerCfg does set obs_groups = {"actor": ["policy"], "critic": ["policy"]} at .../velocity/config/anymal_d/agents/rsl_rl_ppo_cfg.py:25 -- so this is a per-robot omission in the shipped configs, not a framework default. (2) More fundamentally, the environment publishes nowhere for a critic to look: ObservationsCfg in .../velocity/velocity_env_cfg.py declares exactly one group, policy (line 192, class PolicyCfg at 166), and no privileged group at all. So the critic necessarily sees the same vector the actor does, whatever obs_groups says.
where: installed Isaac Lab tree: source/isaaclab_rl/isaaclab_rl/rsl_rl/rl_cfg.py:252; source/isaaclab_tasks/.../locomotion/velocity/config/anymal_c/agents/rsl_rl_ppo_cfg.py (no obs_groups) against .../anymal_d/agents/rsl_rl_ppo_cfg.py:25 (has it); .../velocity/velocity_env_cfg.py:162-192. Inherited unchanged by src/bestiary/isaac/anymal_desert_env_cfg.py, which overrides only scene.terrain.terrain_generator. grep finds obs_groups nowhere in Bestiary src/.
why_it_matters: A privileged critic is one of the standard reasons a sim-trained locomotion policy converges at all -- the critic is allowed to see terrain height, friction, applied disturbances and body states the deployed actor cannot have, which makes its value estimates far less noisy without touching what the actor learns. Inheriting a reward and a hyperparameter set from that literature while silently NOT inheriting the asymmetry means any comparison against published sample efficiency is a comparison against a different algorithm. It also compounds a gap already in the record: a prior refutation noted the shipped ANYmal config carries this, and this run is the first time it applied to our own training rather than to a config we had only read. And the direction of the error is the awkward one -- if a Hound run underperforms the published recipe, the missing critic input is a confound that will not appear in any reward-design argument. See research/learnings/017.
cheapest_next_step: No GPU, and it is a decision before it is a code change. Either (a) declare the asymmetry: add a privileged ObsGroup to the Hound env cfg -- the obvious candidates already exist in the sim and not in the policy vector (per-wheel longitudinal slip, contact forces, the sampled friction, base linear velocity in world frame) -- and set obs_groups = {"actor": ["policy"], "critic": ["policy", "privileged"]}; or (b) state plainly in the Hound agent config that the critic is symmetric and why. Whichever, the assertable part is a check that the two agree: a guard that fails when obs_groups names a group the env does not publish, and when a config claiming asymmetry resolves to a critic input identical to the actor's. Note the width consequence: a privileged group is NOT the policy observation, so it should not move the one-way door the obs-spec hash protects -- worth confirming before assuming it is free.

what: py-spy reported a confident, wrong crash location and misdirected an investigation for several probes. A training process was dying with SIGSEGV (exit 139) about 3 s into Kit startup; py-spy sampled it and reported the stack sitting in set_materialx_paths inside omni.usd.config, which reads as a renderer or Vulkan configuration problem and was chased as one. There was no graphics problem. py-spy had sampled an IDLE THREAD -- a thread parked in a plausible-looking frame, in a process that runs dozens of them. The actual cause came from Kit's breakpad backtrace, which reports the thread that died: pthread_join <- libscipy_openblas...!blas_thread_shutdown_ <- __register_atfork <- __libc_fork <- libomni.platforminfo.plugin.so, i.e. OpenBLAS's atfork handler joining a thread pool that does not exist in a forked child. Fixed by OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1.
where: research/learnings/016-the-ceiling-was-never-in-the-launch-path.md records the mechanism and research/scripts/016_openblas_fork_math.py verifies the OpenBLAS half of the backtrace locally (blas_thread_shutdown_ defined, __register_atfork / pthread_join / pthread_create imported, in venv/.../numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-32a4b2a6.so). why_it_matters: It is an instrument caveat, which is a class this file already carries -- rows 36 (a decomposition that omitted a term), 41 (an eval with no yaw axis), 43 (a hardcoded term list) and 55 (a peak VRAM figure with no instrument). The specific trap: a SAMPLING profiler answers 'where is some thread right now', and a crash is a question about ONE thread at ONE instant, so on a multithreaded process like Kit the two questions have almost nothing to do with each other. The output is not noisy or empty, which is what would make it obviously useless -- it is specific, syntactically perfect and wrong, so it reads exactly like a finding. Same shape as learnings/011, where a plausible failure mode that correlated with a bad number turned out to be 0.9% of it.

where: src/bestiary/isaac/check_hound.py, check_reward_budget_against_011_and_015. The `if half == 0.0: lin_ceiling = 1.0` branch is correct as arithmetic -- it is the limit of the closed form -- and is exactly what inflates the denominator, which is why this is an anomaly and not a bug. what: Collapsing lin_vel_y to (0,0) silently moved the TERRAIN CURRICULUM, not only the reward. In terrain_levels_vel the demote bar is `distance < ||command_xy|| * max_episode_length_s * 0.5`, i.e. proportional to ||c_xy||, while the promote bar is `terrain_generator.size[0] / 2` = 4.0 m and is command-independent. E||c_xy|| fell from 0.765196 over the inherited square to 0.500000 with c_y pinned at zero -- a 34.66% drop in the demote bar with the promote bar unchanged. The committed +/-0.3 range sits at 0.541056, a 29.29% drop. Analytic check on the inherited square: (sqrt(2) + asinh(1)) / 3 = 0.765196.
where: isaaclab_tasks/.../locomotion/velocity/mdp/curriculums.py:42-54 for the two bars; src/bestiary/isaac/hound_desert_env_cfg.py sets the range. All three E||c_xy|| values and both drops are printed by research/scripts/0006_reward_economics_refutation.py section 1.
why_it_matters: A command-range edit reads as a reward change and gets filed as one, but it also changes which ground the machine ends up standing on: a lower demote bar means the same policy demotes less often and equilibrates at a higher terrain level. So any comparison spanning that edit is confounded on terrain difficulty as well as on income, and the confound is invisible in the reward table. Same shape as the terrain-spec invariant in CLAUDE.md -- a ground change that leaves every checkpoint loading and every guard green -- except that here the ground moved via the COMMAND SAMPLER, which no hash covers.
cheapest_next_step: Nothing to build; the rule is the artifact. Recorded so it is findable by grep: a change to any command range is also a change to the terrain curriculum, and a cycle that edits one must state E||c_xy|| before and after. If it becomes worth enforcing, the cheapest guard is an assertion that E||c_xy|| has not moved since the last ledger row for the same env id.

what: NO REWARD TERM PRICES WHEEL TORQUE, so a policy that cruises with a limb leaning on the ground earns full tracking income at literally zero cost. dof_torques_l2 is scoped to LEG_JOINT_EXPR, and the only wheel-scoped term, dof_acc_wheel_l2, prices ACCELERATION -- exactly 0.000000/step at constant speed. The argument that physics prices it anyway (weight on linkage unloads the wheels, traction is proportional to normal load) does not hold: the friction cap is 3.1904 N*m per wheel, demand at the measured 2.0 m/s^2 saturation is 0.7227 N*m (22.65% of the cone), steady cruise needs only the 0.3990 N*m wheel frictionloss (12.51%), and with a limb resting at 40 N the cone is still only 16.5% used at cruise. Top speed is set by a velocity limit and thrust by a wheelie, not by force.
where: src/bestiary/isaac/hound_desert_env_cfg.py (HoundRewardsCfg: dof_torques_l2 and dof_acc_l2 scoped to the legs, dof_acc_wheel_l2 the only wheel term); src/bestiary/robots/hound/check.py:276 records the machine saturating 'with the friction cone barely 5% used' and :321 asserts 'the limit is UNLOADING, not the friction cone'.
